hook: Salt melts at 801 °C, sugar at about 186 °C, sand above 1,700 °C. Copper bends, salt shatters, and graphite smears onto paper. Every one of these differences comes from two questions: what are the particles, and what holds them together?

prereq.q: Why does a solid ionic compound fail to conduct electricity?
options: Its ions are fixed in the lattice
prereq.why: The ions carry charge but cannot move until the solid melts or dissolves.

options: Layers of cations slide within the sea of electrons
prereq.why: Metallic bonding is not tied to particular atoms, so layers slide without breaking it.

prereq.q: Which attraction holds I₂ molecules to each other?
prereq.why: I₂ is nonpolar, so its molecules attract only by dispersion forces.

figure.caption: Ionic, molecular, covalent network and metallic solids, drawn at the particle level.

chain.cause: Molecular solids are separate molecules held only by intermolecular forces
chain.effect: melting overcomes weak attractions, so they melt low and are soft

chain.cause: Molecules carry no net charge and have no free electrons
chain.effect: molecular solids do not conduct in any state

chain.cause: In a covalent network every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbors
chain.effect: melting must break covalent bonds, so network solids melt very high and are very hard

chain.cause: A network's valence electrons are locked in bonds (graphite's layers excepted)
chain.effect: most network solids do not conduct

ideas: Ask what the particles are and what holds them: ions (ionic bonds), cations and electrons (metallic), molecules (IMFs) or atoms (covalent network).
Molecular solids melt low and never conduct; covalent network solids melt very high and are very hard.
Crystalline solids have repeating order and sharp melting points; amorphous solids soften over a range.

misconception.wrong: Molecular solids melt low because their covalent bonds are weak.
misconception.right: Melting a molecular solid breaks no covalent bonds. It only overcomes the intermolecular forces between molecules, which are much weaker than covalent bonds.

summary: Solids are ionic, metallic, molecular or covalent network. Molecular solids are molecules held by intermolecular forces: soft, low-melting and nonconducting. Covalent network solids are one continuous web of covalent bonds: very hard, very high-melting and (except graphite) nonconducting.
